title: CHAPTER XX - OF OFFENCES RELATING TO MARRIAGE
overview: This chapter covers IPC Sections 493-498 and their subject-matter correspondences in BNS Sections 81-84. It distinguishes deceit about an existing lawful marriage, bigamy, concealment of a former marriage, a fraudulent ceremony and taking, enticing, concealing or detaining a married woman with the specified intent. IPC 497 is retained for historical and constitutional study, with its invalidation clearly identified.
objectives: Identify all six IPC entries and the relevant BNS section or constitutional status.
Distinguish belief in an existing lawful marriage from a promise of future marriage.
Apply the elements of bigamy, concealment and the statutory exceptions.
Distinguish a knowingly fraudulent ceremony from a merely invalid marriage.
Explain Joseph Shine and the absence of a BNS adultery counterpart.
Analyse BNS 84 using its act, knowledge and intent requirements.
transition: The relevant BNS provisions commenced on 1 July 2024. Select the substantive law by the date and nature of conduct, BNS 358 repeal-and-savings rules and Article 20(1) of the Constitution; complaint timing alone does not decide the applicable offence or penalty. These marriage offences are reorganised within BNS Chapter V, concerning offences against women and children. IPC Chapter XX is retained as the course heading. IPC 497 was already struck down in 2018: do not confuse constitutional invalidation with the later general repeal of IPC. This chapter ends at IPC 498; cruelty under IPC 498A belongs to the separate Chapter XXA.

groups.title: Section-by-section IPC-to-BNS comparison
groups.explanation: Five IPC entries correspond to four BNS sections because IPC 494 and 495 are consolidated in subsections 82(1) and 82(2). IPC 497 has no BNS counterpart. These notes summarise the cited central texts; the validity of a marriage must be established under the applicable marriage law.

groups.title: Ingredients and practical application
groups.explanation:
Deceit and belief (81): identify the representation that a lawful marriage already exists, its falsity, the resulting belief and cohabitation or intercourse in that belief. An unfulfilled future promise requires a different analysis and must not be mechanically labelled an offence under 81.

Bigamy (82): establish a valid subsisting first marriage and the subsequent marriage in the legally required manner. Identify why the latter is void owing to the living spouse. Check competent-court orders, dates and the applicable marriage law rather than assuming every second relationship is a second marriage.

Seven-year absence exception: continuous absence, no news of being alive during that period, and disclosure of the known facts to the new spouse before marriage must be considered together. Mere non-contact for a short period is insufficient. Do not treat this exception as a general licence based only on a missing-person report.

Fraudulent ceremony (83): an unlawful result alone is insufficient. The section expressly requires a ceremony, knowledge that lawful marriage does not result, and dishonesty or fraudulent intention.

Constitutional distinction: Joseph Shine protects equality, dignity and sexual autonomy against the former adultery offence. Matrimonial relief and independently proved criminal offences are different questions. BNS 84 must be assessed on its own words, not used to assume criminality merely because a married woman forms a relationship.

Evidence for a problem answer: identify the applicable marriage law, proof of required ceremonies or formalities, any dissolution or nullity order, disclosure or concealment, communications explaining the alleged deceit and the conduct alleged. These are analytical prompts, not a substitute for the statutory burden of proof.

keyPoints: IPC 493 -> BNS 81: deceit causing belief in an existing lawful marriage and resulting cohabitation or intercourse.
IPC 494 -> BNS 82(1): bigamy; maximum seven years and fine, subject to the statutory exception.
IPC 495 -> BNS 82(2): underlying bigamy plus concealment; maximum ten years and fine.
IPC 496 -> BNS 83: knowingly fraudulent or dishonest marriage ceremony; maximum seven years and fine.
IPC 497: struck down in Joseph Shine on 27 September 2018; no BNS adultery counterpart.
IPC 498 -> BNS 84: specified taking, enticing, concealment or detention with the statutory knowledge and intent; maximum two years or fine or both.
Disclosure alone does not validate a prohibited second marriage; apply the complete exception.
A failed marriage, relationship or promise is not automatically proof of a criminal offence.
examFocus: Start with the conduct date and applicable statute. Identify the precise representation, marriage, ceremony or taking/enticing/concealment/detention. Prove every required mental element and causal link. For bigamy, establish both marriages under the applicable law and test the statutory exception. For adultery, state the constitutional holding and absence of a BNS counterpart rather than reproducing the former offence as current law. End with the correct subsection and punishment.

practice.question: A man deceitfully induces a woman to believe they are already lawfully married, and she cohabits with him in that belief. Which provision applies?
practice.answer: Analyse BNS 81 (formerly IPC 493). Prove deceit, absence of lawful marriage, the induced belief and cohabitation or intercourse in that belief. The maximum imprisonment is ten years with liability to fine.

practice.question: Does living together with a second partner automatically prove bigamy?
practice.answer: No. BNS 82(1) requires a subsequent marriage void because of a living spouse. Establish the subsisting first marriage and legally relevant proof of the second under the applicable marriage law.

practice.question: A spouse has been absent for seven years. Is that fact alone sufficient for the exception?
practice.answer: No. Examine continuous absence, whether the person heard of the spouse as alive within that time, and disclosure of known real facts to the new spouse before the subsequent marriage.

practice.question: What does concealment add under BNS 82(2)?
practice.answer: It aggravates an established offence under 82(1) where the former marriage is concealed from the new spouse. The maximum rises from seven to ten years, with liability to fine. Concealment does not replace proof of the underlying offence.

practice.question: An invalid ceremony occurred through an honest misunderstanding. Is BNS 83 automatically established?
practice.answer: No. The statutory knowledge and dishonest or fraudulent intention must be proved. Invalidity by itself is insufficient.

practice.question: Can IPC 497 be treated as an operative offence with a new BNS number?
practice.answer: No. Joseph Shine struck it down in 2018, and BNS contains no adultery counterpart. Separate matrimonial consequences or other offences require their own legal analysis.

practice.question: How does BNS 84 differ from simply alleging an adulterous relationship?
practice.answer: It requires a specified act of taking, enticing, concealing or detaining, the required knowledge or reason to believe about marriage, and the stated intent. An allegation of a relationship alone is not proof of all those elements.

practice.question: Is a promise to marry next year the same as deceit that a lawful marriage already exists?
practice.answer: No. BNS 81 concerns belief in an existing lawful marriage followed by cohabitation or intercourse in that belief. Other allegations require independent analysis under any separately applicable provision.

sources.title: Joseph Shine v. Union of India, 27 September 2018, [2018] 11 SCR 765 - official court-hosted judgment
